items.body: Spike Hellis Successor Over-Pop Spike Hellis’ self-titled 2022 debut LP was wild, unpredictable and unexpected. Part of what made the Los Angeles duo’s take on gnarly mutant body music feel so nervy and dangerous was its aggressive switch-ups, slamming from funky EBM into anxious synthscapes and moody sample cut-ups, all anchored by Lainey Chang and Cortland Gibson’s rancorous vocals. Paired with their furious live shows, which featured the duo crawling over a jungle gym of equipment while a neon sign invited you to dial 1-888-FKN-WEAK, it made Spike Hellis impossible to ignore. Chang and Gibson’s new LP Successor takes all the spite, all the sweat, and all the smart programming and arrangement that made them so compelling, and boils it down to an even more potent and addictive formulation. It manages the trick of being both very minimal and absolutely enormous; at any given moment there could be little more than a bassline, a sample and a smattering percussion sounds going on, but each of those disparate elements is tuned and positioned for maximum impact. Debut single “By God” places a funky cowbell and crushed synth stabs on top of its burbling synth bass for one of the most addictive grooves of the year, and that’s before the shouted and sung vocals lob the song into brand new territory. Simultaneously, the Art-of-Noise-through-a-mirror-darkly “Entirely Mine” folds its repeated vocal samples into new shapes, ardent and punchy, but also steady and focused. The sheer power of the record lies in its meticulous arrangement, how everything is placed in the mix, and the space left between each drum hit, shout, sample, or synth note. “Your Successor” doesn’t sound complicated, but there’s a wealth of variation in how Chang’s half-rapped vocals bounce off the off-kilter drum programming, the stereo spread of the slow moving background textures and the tiny ripples of digital artifacting that flow into the outro. It’s none of it accidental, whether at their most noisy (“Pareplaneta”, which explodes and then lets you sit uncomfortably in the echoes) or their most accessible (the surprisingly touching “Pillow Talk”, whose bright chirps and barks manage to sound melancholic) every element is purposeful, and adds to the strength of the whole. And that’s all before we get into how ferocious and ornery Chang and Gibson are on the mic. And what’s more, that ire is cutting, and as refined and strategic as any other aspect of the album. There’s a genuine meanness to the sing-songy chorus of “Temptation” (“Feels like every time we turn around/these two petty fuckers run their mouths”) that suggests that whoever Hellis are addressing knows they’re being called out and would do well to duck them going forward. It’s a sort of calm antipathy that can be righteous (“Enemy Lines”), menacing (“Unwound (Get Right)”), or disdainful (“No Bite”), but is never obnoxious, no matter how spicy or bitter it might come across. Successor is Spike Hellis distilled; all the raw energy, all the movement, all the combativeness of their debut is here, but made sleeker, and delivered in more calculated fashion. And bizarrely, it ends up being both bracingly intense, and a whole lot of fun to listen to. It shouldn’t be possible to sound this unbothered and cool and this savage at the same time, but here we are; Spike Hellis are working hard, but you’ll never see them sweat. Highly recommended. Buy it. Successor by Spike Hellis The post Spike Hellis, “Successor” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 発行年：2026 版元：けはい出版 公式サイト：https://withdilemma.theshop.jp/items/141822340 『交差点で：デザイン、言語、経験』はビジュアルコミュニケーションデザイナー、環境活動家の平山みな美によるインタビュー集である。横浜を拠点とする独立出版社兼印刷所NEUTRAL COLORSの依頼で、彼女がオランダの文化施設で滞在制作を行なった際の成果物として制作された。 「主に気候変動、環境問題、ジェンダー不平等などに取り組む団体や企業のデザインを率先して引き受けている★1」平山であるが、そんな問題意識をこの滞在でも深めようと、取材対象との対話に際し「文化的な表象という言葉を聞いて、思い浮かべるオブジェクトを持ってきてほしい★2」と伝え、それをきっかけとした議論が同書には収められている。この「文化的な表象」というテーマはきわめて広範であり、話題が抽象的になってしまう可能性もあるだろう。しかし平山は具体的に対象を「名指す」よう提案することによって、その懸念を回避している。 対話に応じた6組の活動はさまざまだ。むしろ「デザイン」という領域をメインのフ
items.body: 発行年：2026 版元：けはい出版 公式サイト：https://withdilemma.theshop.jp/items/141822340 『交差点で：デザイン、言語、経験』はビジュアルコミュニケーションデザイナー、環境活動家の平山みな美によるインタビュー集である。横浜を拠点とする独立出版社兼印刷所NEUTRAL COLORSの依頼で、彼女がオランダの文化施設で滞在制作を行なった際の成果物として制作された。 「主に気候変動、環境問題、ジェンダー不平等などに取り組む団体や企業のデザインを率先して引き受けている★1」平山であるが、そんな問題意識をこの滞在でも深めようと、取材対象との対話に際し「文化的な表象という言葉を聞いて、思い浮かべるオブジェクトを持ってきてほしい★2」と伝え、それをきっかけとした議論が同書には収められている。この「文化的な表象」というテーマはきわめて広範であり、話題が抽象的になってしまう可能性もあるだろう。しかし平山は具体的に対象を「名指す」よう提案することによって、その懸念を回避している。 対話に応じた6組の活動はさまざまだ。むしろ「デザイン」という領域をメインのフィールドとしているのは、ルーベン・パター（Ruben Pater）ぐらいと言ってもいいかもしれない。彼にしても『The Politics of Design』（BIS Publishers、2016）のようにデザインが孕む政治性、権力性について書いた著作があり、さまざまな活動に取り組んでいる。平山の依頼に応じたのは他にキュレーション集団、グループなど多様であり、複数のアウトプット──書店、出版、展示、社会運動など──に取り組んでいるケースが多い。 彼／彼女たちのアクチュアルで柔軟なアプローチについては実際に本を参照されたいが、印象に残ったのは女性やノンバイナリーアーティストを支援するイニシアチブのグローイング・ペインズ（Growing Pains）のメンバーが持参した文化的表象である。彼女たちが対話の起点としたのは、オランダの税務局が使用する封筒だった。 オランダでは育児給付金制度を悪用し、不正に受給した後国外逃亡した詐欺事件が2013年に発覚した。そして政府はその後、対策として「二重国籍者、主に西洋風でない姓を持つ者、そしてひとり親家庭を特に標的とするシステムを導入★3」する。AIも使われていたというこの人種差別的なシステムによって、オランダでは何千もの家族が身に覚えのない詐欺の告発にあい、給付金の返還を求められたのである。 18年にこのスキャンダルは発覚し、関与した内閣は失脚したが、人種によるプロファイリングは制度の一部に未だ残り続けているとグローイング・ペインズのジュニア・スヴェンスチンスカヤは語る。オランダの国章がビジュアルアイデンティティとして小さめに印刷され、簡素なタイポグラフィで構成されたこの税務局の封筒は、極めて事務的で「モダン」なデザインである。しかし、その背後にはアルゴリズムとして組み込まれた人種バイアスがあり、そこにある権力を──結果的に──表わしているのである。 ★1──平山みな美編『交差点で：デザイン、言語、経験』（けはい出版、2026、13ページ） ★2──同上、7ページ ★3──同上、91ページ （後編へ）※8/17公開予定 執筆日：2026/05/15（金）

items.album: 高嶋慈｜「路上、お邪魔ですか？」展を起点に考える──路上と表現・公共性（後編）
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/04/25～2026/09/06 会場：金沢21世紀美術館［石川県］ 公式サイト：https://www.kanazawa21.jp/data_list.php?g=65&d=1852 （中編より） 前編の末尾で指摘したように、「路上、お邪魔ですか？」展における根本的な問題は、2020年に渋谷で起きた路上生活者殺害事件の加害者が発した「 彼女・・が邪魔だった」という言葉をタイトルに参照しつつも、展示内容において「ホームレスの女性」が透明化・排除され、ジェンダーの視点から「路上」を考える視点がまったく欠落していることにある。不特定多数の人々が行き交う路上は、ジェンダーにおいて決してニュートラルな空間ではない。むしろ、どのようなジェンダー（と見なされる）かによって、誰からどのような眼差しを向けられるのか（性的欲望なのか無関心なのか警戒なのか蔑視なのか）という経験がまったく異なり、それに付随して「路上を歩くこと」の安全度も危険度も異なってくる。つまり本展は、「路上、お邪魔ですか？」と掲げているが、路上で実際に「お前は邪魔だ」と 排除されない・・・・・・人の視線で企画されている
items.body: 会期：2026/04/25～2026/09/06 会場：金沢21世紀美術館［石川県］ 公式サイト：https://www.kanazawa21.jp/data_list.php?g=65&d=1852 （中編より） 前編の末尾で指摘したように、「路上、お邪魔ですか？」展における根本的な問題は、2020年に渋谷で起きた路上生活者殺害事件の加害者が発した「 彼女・・が邪魔だった」という言葉をタイトルに参照しつつも、展示内容において「ホームレスの女性」が透明化・排除され、ジェンダーの視点から「路上」を考える視点がまったく欠落していることにある。不特定多数の人々が行き交う路上は、ジェンダーにおいて決してニュートラルな空間ではない。むしろ、どのようなジェンダー（と見なされる）かによって、誰からどのような眼差しを向けられるのか（性的欲望なのか無関心なのか警戒なのか蔑視なのか）という経験がまったく異なり、それに付随して「路上を歩くこと」の安全度も危険度も異なってくる。つまり本展は、「路上、お邪魔ですか？」と掲げているが、路上で実際に「お前は邪魔だ」と 排除されない・・・・・・人の視線で企画されている。 「ホームレスの女性」という何重にも周縁化された存在に言及する現代美術作品が、まったく存在しないわけではない。例えば、2003年より東京都内の公園のブルーテント村に住み、2007年にホームレスの女性たちのグループ「ノラ」を立ち上げたいちむらみさこは、自身の日常生活と制作を地続きとしながら、ジェンダー、貧困、ジェントリフィケーションの問題に取り組んでいる★1。「Family」シリーズ（2013）では、テント村、近代異性愛家族や家父長制を象徴する「家」、家の内部にある墓、女性の身体、燃える炎などが赤い絵具で描かれたドローイングとともに、路上の映像が投影される★2。 以下では、本展出品作以外の作品や複数の論考を参照し、歴史的視座を交えて、ジェンダーやセクシュアリティの視点から「路上を歩くこと」の制約と権利について考える。フェミニズム美術史家グリゼルダ・ポロックは、古典的著作『視線と差異 フェミニズムで読む美術史』所収の論考「女性性（フェミニニティ）の空間とモダニティ」において、マネや印象派の男性画家と、ベルト・モリゾとメアリー・カサットという二人の印象派の女性画家が描いた「空間」の差異を分析することで、モダニティが、性と階級を二重に分離する複雑な政治的力学によって駆動していることを指摘した★3。モリゾとカサットの絵画に多く描かれたのは、食堂、客間、寝室、バルコニー、庭など、女性に割り当てられた家庭内の私的な空間である（モデルも家族や友人、使用人など私的な関係にある女性たちが多い）。家庭外の公的な空間を描いた作品もあるが、公園の散歩や劇場での観劇など、ブルジョワ階級が余暇を誇示する社交の空間に限定される。また、ポロックは、モリゾ作品では、欄干、バルコニー、堤防といった境界線によって、ひとつの画面が二つの空間体系に分離されるとともに、絵のなかの女性たちが「境界線の内側」の私的領域に閉じ込められていることに着目する。つまり、欄干やバルコニーは、公的空間と私的空間の境界に加え、男性性の空間と女性性の空間の境界でもあるという二重の象徴性を帯びている。 一方、マネや印象派の男性画家たちは、バーやカフェ、キャバレーという歓楽の場や、劇場の舞台裏、娼館すなわち金銭を介した性的交換の場に自由に出入りし、描くことができた。だが、ブルジョワ階級の女性がこうした場所へ立ち入ることは「品位を汚す行為」として禁止され、夫や付き添いの女性を伴わずにひとりで外出することも（娼婦と見なされるという）危険を伴い、不道徳な行為とみなされた。したがって、ヴァルター・ベンヤミンが『パサージュ論』で描いた、群衆のなかをそぞろ歩き、近代都市のスペクタクルな消費空間を心ゆくまで眺める「遊歩者」とは、男性に限定されたモデルであるとポロックは指摘する。つまり、モダニティとは、公私の領域を男性性と女性性に割り当てたうえで、処女／娼婦、子どもを産む女／性的欲望の対象としての女という二極のセクシュアリティに女性を分離して階級化する、性と階級が複雑に絡み合う政治的力学に支えられている。 だが、ポロック自身「モダニティはまだわれわれとともにある」と述べるように、こうした支配構造は過去のものではない。「女性性の空間はいまも女の生活を規制し、その規制は、街中で無遠慮な男の視線の攻撃を浴びることから卑劣な強姦までさまざまである」★4。この事例として、ローリー・アンダーソンの《Fully Automated Nikon（Object / Objection / Objectivity）》（1973）が挙げられる★5。アンダーソンは、フルオートのカメラの機動性を活かし、路上で性的なからかい目的で声をかけてきた男性を撮影し、状況を綴ったテクストを添えて展示した。「写真とテクスト」というコンセプチュアル・アートの王道を踏襲しつつ、見る／見られるというジェンダーの非対称性を転倒させ、女性の身体が客体化（Object）されることに対する異議申し立て（Objection）を痛烈に行なっている。また、被写体の男性の「目」に白いテープを貼って隠す操作も多義的な批評性を示す。「プライバシーの配慮」を装いつつ、「ちょっとしたいたずら」ではなく「犯罪」であると明示し、さらに彼を「匿名化」することで、こうした性犯罪がいたるところで無数に行なわれている遍在性をも示唆する。そして、「見られる対象」に置かれた男性は、女性の身体を無遠慮に眺めまわす有害な視線をも封じられているのだ。 最後に、「路上を安全に歩くこと」の権利は（シスジェンダーの）女性だけの問題に限らないこと、そして「歩く行為」が安全性の保障に加えて、連帯の可能性に開かれていることについて、哲学者・クィア理論家のジュディス・バトラーの論考を参照して考えたい。路上を歩く行為は、抗議活動に加えて、社会から不可視化された存在が「ここにいる」ことを自らの実存をもって示すための切実な手段でもある。だが、セクシュアル・マイノリティは、プライドパレードという祝祭的で非日常的な瞬間 にだけ ・・・ 、路上空間に姿を現わすわけではない。とりわけトランスジェンダーは、公共空間を歩くだけで、好奇や侮蔑の視線をジロジロと無遠慮に向けられ、侮蔑的な言葉を見知らぬ他人から浴びせられ、ときには身体的な暴力を受ける。言い換えれば、トランスジェンダーが公共空間を（精神的にも）安全に歩けるかどうかは、単にそのトランス個人の問題ではなく、同じ場所を歩いている人が「トランスが安全に歩ける権利を支持している」と表明しているかどうかにかかっている。バトラーは、『アセンブリ: 行為遂行性・複数性・政治』において、次のように述べる。 日常生活そのものが暴力の恐怖なしで成立し、保護されていなくても安全に歩けるようになるとすれば、間違いなくそれは、たとえその権利がたった一人によって行使される場合でさえ、多くの人々がその権利を支持しているからだ。（中略）歩くことは、ここはトランスジェンダーの人々が歩く公共空間である、ここは様々な形式の衣服を身にまとった人々が、どのようにジェンダー化されていようと、あるいはどの宗教を表明していようと、暴力に脅えることなく自由に移動できる公共空間である、と述べることなのである★6。 デモやパレードといった一時的で非日常的な行為に限らず、「歩くこと」は、特定の誰かを 排除しない ・・・・・ という姿勢を無言のうちに、自らの身体を通して日常的に示す連帯の行為にもなりうる。政治と日常性は矛盾しない。むしろ、日常的な歩行の行為のうちにも、政治性や連帯の意思は宿るのだ、という気づきこそが求められている。 ★1──いちむらみさこ『ホームレスでいること 見えるものと見えないもののあいだ』（創元社、2024） ★2──吉岡恵美子・伊藤まゆみ編『越境 : 収蔵作品とゲストアーティストがひらく視座 : 京都精華大学ギャラリーリニューアル記念展』（京都精華大学、2022） ★3──グリゼルダ・ポロック『視線と差異 フェミニズムで読む美術史』（萩原弘子訳、ちくま学芸文庫、2025、pp.151-232） ★4──同上、p.230 ★5──村上由鶴『アートとフェミニズムは誰のもの？』（光文社、2023、pp.219-223）。ヘレナ・レキット編、ペギー・フェラン概説『アート&フェミニズム』（鈴木奈々訳、ファイドン、2005、p.96） ★6──ジュディス・バトラー『アセンブリ : 行為遂行性・複数性・政治』（佐藤嘉幸・清水知子訳、青土社、2018、pp.69-70）なお、引用箇所の訳の太字部分は下記を参照した。山田秀頌「バトラーとトランスの両義的な関係」（『現代思想』2019年3月臨時増刊号、pp.192-205） 鑑賞日：2026/06/20（土） 関連レビュー items.body: IUGA‘s debut album Meldrop is an intensely personal meditation on grief, nature and renewal, rooted in the forests of the Tuscan Apennines where the composer now lives. Inspired by the loss of his dog Toki and by the untamed landscape surrounding his home, the record traces an emotional journey in which wolves, deer, birds, snakes and humans inhabit the same fragile ecosystem. The title refers to the final drop left hanging from a runny nose after tears have run dry—a striking image that becomes a metaphor for grief persisting long after mourning appears to have subsided. There are no dramatic gestures here. The album is driven by atmosphere rather than narrative, favouring gradual shifts in mood over overt climaxes. “Unleash (Into la Rata)” immediately immerses the listener in unfamiliar territory, its fractured voices and restless modular textures creating a palpable sense of unease. “Toki” follows with a restrained lament whose melodic contours suggest farewell rather than despair. “Tail” picks up where the opening track leaves off, but with less disquiet. Having become acclimatised to the album’s sonic environment, the listener begins to find points of orientation. The tension returns in “Into Your Gaze”, where an electronically distorted voice seems to communicate from Hades. Yet expectations are constantly overturned. “Aspis” is unexpectedly calm and measured, acknowledging nature’s indifference without turning it into violence. Just when “Hurst” seems to open the possibility of tranquillity and reconciliation, the closing title track allows the drone to gather force before gradually dissipating, suggesting that grief never truly disappears but becomes part of one’s emotional landscape. Although Meldrop is created entirely with analogue and modular synthesis, it rarely feels technological. IUGA approaches his instruments instinctively, treating them almost as living organisms rather than machines. Recorded with minimal editing and almost no post-production, the album preserves the rawness of performance, allowing metallic resonances, unstable oscillations and breathing textures to evoke the physical presence of the forest itself. The result is a debut that resists sentimentality while remaining deeply affecting: an album in which grief is neither conquered nor romanticised, but gradually absorbed into the wider rhythms of the natural world. To shed further light on Meldrop, IUGA kindly answered a few questions by email. Meldrop is described as an album about the place you call home, your dogs, the forest and the lives that inhabit it. The record often feels like an ecosystem in which different forms of life coexist. How did the landscape around you shape the music, and were there specific encounters, sounds or memories that found their way into an album which, as the liner notes indicate is, at least partially, shaped by personal grief? Meldrop is deeply connected to the place where I’ve been living for about four years now, a magical, wild spot in the mountains outside Florence. I can say with certainty that without this place, this album wouldn’t exist. The opening track, “Unleash (Into la Rata),” marks my entrance into the house in the woods. I finally felt free, unleashed, but also overwhelmed by the wilderness and the life thriving within it. I tried to convey in music the sensation of wolves pushing up to the thresholds of my home and their howling at dusk, echoing across the entire valley. The spectacular concert of nocturnal birds, whose spectral songs accompanied me to sleep, the sheer wonder of rediscovering hundreds, thousands of fireflies after so many years, having believed they were gone forever. The meaning of Meldrop is “a drop at the tip of the nose / a runny nose”, and it’s tied to the loss of my dog, which happened the year after I moved here. The entire album revolves around this, and the track “Toki” is dedicated to her, or rather, to us. It’s my farewell, her funeral, the moments leading up to her burial, when I carried her in my arms from my house to the spot I had chosen just a few meters away. In that moment, those few meters felt like hundreds of kilometers, and when even the tears had run dry, only that drop at my nose, that meldrop, was left. It stayed with me for hours, days, even months. That’s why I speak of a fragile emotional reconstruction, so much of my energy in the following months was spent finding myself again, forgiving myself, and rebuilding a new beginning. Toki died from an asp bite; in my mind, the track “Aspis” tells the story of that day when their paths crossed, and consequently, mine did too. The sound builds up in a crescendo, its intensity rising to a climax that marks the final, fatal strike by the viper. It took a long time to understand that nature is also this, that awe and wonder don’t just manifest in its beauty, but also in its cruelty, and that there is no right or wrong in nature. Everything is in its place, every life follows its course. The album explores birth, life, death and what you describe as a realm where “even death becomes solely a matter of sound and scent.” That is a striking image. How did you approach translating such deeply physical and sensory experiences into a language of modular synthesis and ambient composition, especially when working without conventional narrative or lyrics? Also, what do the vocals concealed in the track “Into your gaze” refer to? Are they intedend as a warning? Modular synthesis was the only necessary path for composing these tracks, it allows me to know myself deeply and establish a conversation with my inner self. I always say that I don’t play my instruments, but rather I play with them, manipulating and letting myself be manipulated by the living sound, so as to respect its intrinsic, primal electricity. Since this is a deeply personal album, I needed to feel completely honest, first and foremost with myself, but also with the listener. I tried to convey my lived experience, my emotions, and the surrounding environment through these “machines,” often letting myself sink into long nighttime sessions lasting hours and hours, solely in search of sonorities that would come into contact with the most hidden and fragile part of me, the part that ultimately gave birth to the album. “Into Your Gaze” is a very difficult track for me to analyze, somewhat like the entire album. If you try to analyze everything you won’t come out a winner, but if you let yourself be carried away, you do. I’ll try to help with a cinematic example from one of my favorite directors, Lars von Trier. In a scene from the film Antichrist, the protagonist, during one of his frequent walks in the woods, spots among the vegetation a wounded and bloodied fox. The animal lies hidden, biting and tearing at its own flesh, self-devouring. Turning its gaze toward the protagonist, it roars in an infernal voice: “Chaos reigns.” With “Into Your Gaze,” I wanted to convey that exact same sensation you get when watching that scene. I wanted to show the dark, infinitely powerful side of nature that doesn’t obey human logic, and that is very often governed by a blind destructiveness to which the human being can only submit. The title, on the other hand, in contrast to these dark forces, comes from my encounters in the woods with wild animals, especially deer, foxes and, more rarely, nocturnal birds of prey. There is a moment when our eyes lock, and I am in your gaze, and you are in mine. In that precious moment, I vanish, I am matter, I am nature. It’s a gesture of light that touches my core and restores my balance. The same goes, though on a more frequent basis, with my dogs. Being in their gaze makes me feel at home every single time. Toki Although Meldrop is built entirely from analogue and modular synthesizers, it rarely feels technological. Instead, it conveys something organic, almost animalistic, as if the machines themselves were breathing or responding to the environment. What attracts you to modular synthesis as a tool for expressing themes of nature, grief and memory, and how much of the album emerged through improvisation versus careful construction? I’m really glad that this feeling comes through. This wild imagery stems directly from the nature I inhabit, and managing to convey something organic and animalistic, as you say, was the goal of this album from the very start. I believe much of this result is due to my approach with modular synthesis: I have a deep aversion to academic studying and technicalities, I hate reading manuals, and I hate practicing by studying every single module and its specifications. I let myself be guided by the sound, I explore like a child on an adventure. I delve into the search for sounds in an animalistic way, yes, guided by instinct and primal need. It’s just like when I abandon myself in the woods with my dogs: we are part of the environment, we take our time to scout around, respecting the place we are in and its inhabitants. In the exact same way, I respect the sound and my creative process, without forcing anything, without planning a single thing. I step into my sonic forest and let myself be cradled. No, there was no meticulous construction at all, quite the opposite, in fact. I recorded everything on an old, heroic computer from 2006 that can barely run the recording software, let alone heavy modern plug-ins. This self-imposed limitation helped me get straight to the heart of my sounds, which are intentionally rudimentary, with an almost metallic and primitive feel. There was very little, almost zero, multitrack recording, no sampled sounds (except for the vocal recording on “Into Your Gaze”), and minimal post-production. Even regarding the opening track “Unleash (Into la Rata),” the quasi-animal shouts echoing through it are entirely produced by modular synths, specifically by the Tabor oscillator from the Italian brand Jolin Lab. It was essential for me to create every single sound through careful research and experimentation. The cover artwork by Bernardo Lupo Migone is immediately arresting: a solitary figure suspended in free fall, caught somewhere between descent and flight. It seems to resonate strongly with the album’s themes of loss, transformation and surrender to forces beyond one’s control. How did that image become associated with Meldrop, and what does the falling figure represent to you in relation to the music? When I saw that image for the first time I immediately said, “there it is, I found it”. It’s an incredibly strong, high-impact image. The caption read, “A body moves through space and time”, and that’s exactly it. This suspended figure is still, yet it moves. I was fascinated by the fact that it could be interpreted in different ways. For instance, some might see it as a fall, while others see it as a leap into the void, intentional, brave, and liberating. In any case, the time had come for me to fall; the moment had arrived to free myself from certain fears I had been dragging around for too long, to heal from the grief of losing my beloved dog, and to deeply embrace my pain. To embrace this “mal di vivere”, this existential malaise, that too often has been a heavy burden, deciding for once to transform it into something beautiful through my music. Bernardo Lupo Migone is a talented photographer and a delightful person who was immediately supportive and enthusiastic about being part of the project. Without his imagery, the album wouldn’t have carried the same meaning; he made this debut of mine even more special. Finally, I would like to thank Raffaele Pezzella, founder and curator of the label Unexplained Sounds Group, who believed in this project from the very first listen. He showed courage and intellectual integrity, evaluating solely the quality of my work rather than who I was, how many followers I had, how many albums I had produced, or how many “cool” places I had played. He believed in my music, and given the times we live in, that is something we can’t take for granted. Emerging artists need exactly this: someone who believes in their project regardless of who you are or the numbers you pull. There is a need for truth, to rediscover the essence of sound. There is a need to give voice and support to those who deserve a release through their music and not through the construction of a persona. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Overflowing delivers an oceanic body of shifting harmonies, melodious vibes, and cool, soft-rock resonances. Sparse textural ambient motifs punctuate the ensemble, as in the granular and free-flowing “Sunbird.” Emotionally, the music is entirely connected with hope and gentle bitterness. An oceanic body of shifting harmonies Brad Deschamps is a busy sound artist and talented producer involved in numerous projects (anthéne, North Atlantic Drift, Rosales), highly appreciated by avid listeners of craft-based ambient music and beyond. I had the pleasure of listening to and reviewing a handful of albums he has made, and more generally releases from his labels Polar Seas and Floralia. Polar Seas now stands among the major indie labels with an interest in organic and chamber-like ambient music, alongside Home Normal, Past Inside The Present, Hibernate, Sound in Silence, and Dead Pilots. In this regard, the cassette rewild (published on Floralia) was a marvelous, emotional, and profound musical voyage to the confines of micro-noise and instrumental post-rock ambient, augmented by lamenting vocals, an experience close to Loren Connors‘ Hell’s Kitchen Park. Irresistible sentimental spleen and “happy-sad” hymns. This project, called Early Moon, is actually not far from what you can hear on rewild, built around shoegazing and vibrant aerial guitar moods but with more emphasis on rock elements through the presence of Andrew Eyles (bass, percussion). The result is far from being fully dedicated ambient music, yet there are hints of North Atlantic Drift in the meandering, textured, and engaging instrumental guitar sections that paint inner landscapes. Overflowing delivers an oceanic body of shifting harmonies, melodious vibes, and cool, soft-rock resonances. Sparse textural ambient motifs punctuate the ensemble, as in the granular and free-flowing “Sunbird.” Emotionally, the music is entirely connected with hope and gentle bitterness. Once more, whether working solo or in collaboration, Brad Deschamps does not disappoint. A delicate semi-ambient rock album of alluring reflectiveness, it is easily recommended for fans of Mono, This Will Destroy You, Pan American, Michael Rother (some passages of Sterntaler), and Seeland by Neu! (1975). Overflowing is available on Polar Seas. [Bandcamp] Overflowing by Early MoonThe post Early Moon :: Overflowing (Polar Seas) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Each Monolake release is, of course, sui generis with a context and sound never to recur, but Interstate is unique in its way—document of a vital musical and cultural moment capturing paradigm shifts in (pre-)millennial music production; its deep textured electronics and ever-morphing cyber-rhythms a snapshot of two phonauts boundary-surfing with then cutting edge tech, causing ripples that became waves that would break over the ’00s and beyond. Interstate teems with insectoid detail and dizzying depth of field Interstate by Monolake   The ’90s: an arena for innovative endeavor, in electronic music more than most domains, a simultaneously post- and pre- context eliciting hark-back feed-forward works from e.g. Aphex Twin, Autechre and Boards of Canada that felt, differently, futurist. Likewise Zeitgeist-wise was Interstate, dub techno/ambient electronica duo Monolake’s second album—the last with Gerhard Behles, who left here (1999) to focus on developing the ground-breaking Ableton Live, leaving Robert Henke solo. It started at Technische Universität Berlin—two programming students, early adopters in a burgeoning digital scene, writing music in Max. It would influence the local scene in Berlin and beyond, preparing the ground for Ableton Live—1999 also saw Ableton founded by Henke and Behles with software engineer Bernd Roggendorf. The rest is Geschichte… In this light then may be seen the choice of Interstate as first vinyl in Field Records’ Monolake reissue program. Truly seminal, essential for dub techno and ambient electronica heads alike, along with the reissues of Hong Kong (2008) (see igloo-‘view), compiling the early Chain Reaction EPs, and Gravity (2025) (see igloo-’view); among the most idiosyncratic works where dub techno, microsound and hyperreal electronica intersect, the duo cemented a vision of a quasi-organic post-techno crossing club-home-’phones via a custom sound design and syncopated beats mix. Max/MSP enabled envelope-pushing into vibrant forms where rhythm and sound move in mysterious ways. “Abundance” sets tone, gaseous atmo solidifying into click-y rhythmicity, whirrs and judders cycling echoically into the aether in a fuzz-wash haze. “Gecko”’s full-on techery creates almost total mechanicity (mechanicCity?), electric chirp meshing with birdsong bleeps. “Tangent I” and “Tangent II” hitch roiling low-end to layered synth, “I” with liquid textures like digital drizzle and chattering percussive hiss, “II” with heftier metallic parts, its head-nod slashed with springy stabs. “Perpetuum”’s electro pong workout cedes to “Amazon”’s tract of neo-virtual reality, then “Ginza” and “Terminal” abstract d’n’b geometry into a sleek dub-inflected design. Throughout Interstate teems with insectoid detail and dizzying depth of field, the two like Circe in circuitry conjuring from code immersive spaces as deft in kinesis as they are questing in timbre. Each Monolake release is, of course, sui generis with a context and sound never to recur, but Interstate is unique in its way—document of a vital musical and cultural moment capturing paradigm shifts in (pre-)millennial music production; its deep textured electronics and ever-morphing cyber-rhythms a snapshot of two phonauts boundary-surfing with then cutting edge tech, causing ripples that became waves that would break over the ’00s and beyond. items.body: This music tells of the passage of time, with sparse humorous and facetious tones punctuating the moodier ensemble. Each track is elaborated and designed as a subtle, sentient vignette in the mind of a daydreaming smoker and ordinary thinker who opens his soul and invites the listener to witness his hope, fear, despair, and intricate yet playful reflections. A slow journey through existential wandering 20 Cigarettes by Jesper Møller Nielsen   French indie net label with a substantial production, navigating from lo-fi electronics and leftfield minimalism to noisy soundscapes and atmospheric alt-pop, Lotophagus Records offers here a new album by guitarist and sound explorer Jesper Moller Nielsen. The compositions are based on the spoken words and personal diary of multidirectional intermedia artist Jordane Prestrot, known for his essentially narrative-focused experimental works, often using poetry and irony as their main ingredients. The album evolves as a slow journey through existential wandering, anecdotal and reflective situations. Each smoked cigarette represents a distinct personal life moment, suggesting a state of mind and various encounters with oneself. The minimal, deliberately rough-hewn guitar patterns are articulated around thoughts translated through spoken words, while various sonic explorations, effects, and processed field recordings enhance the album’s narrative purpose. This music tells of the passage of time, with sparse humorous and facetious tones punctuating the moodier ensemble. Each track is elaborated and designed as a subtle, sentient vignette in the mind of a daydreaming smoker and ordinary thinker who opens his soul and invites the listener to witness his hope, fear, despair, and intricate yet playful reflections. There is something in this album that evokes the literary wanderings and explorations of consciousness found in Italo Svevo. In itself, the music and its fragmented, bluesy melodies in slow motion suggest feelings akin to those found in road movies, notably the films of Jim Jarmusch. 20 Cigarettes is recommended for fans of desolate guitar microsounds, field recordings, and evocative, semi-improvised ambiences in the spirit of Loren Connors & David Grubbs, Western Grey, Luca Nasciuti, and Sqürl. 20 Cigarettes is available on Lotophagus. items.album: Ibukun Sunday :: Olùsìn [Worshippers] (Phantom Limb)
items.excerpt: Olùsìn [Worshippers] moves with the gravity of a procession seen from a great distance: slow synth masses, vocal apparitions, soft percussive grammar, low harmonic pressure, field material absorbed into the body of the music. A personal idea of music as spiritual perception Olùsìn [Worshippers] by Ibukun sunday   Lagos born, North London based violist, sound artist and electronic composer Ibukun Sunday has slowly shaped one of the most singular languages in contemporary Afro ambient music.
items.body: Olùsìn [Worshippers] moves with the gravity of a procession seen from a great distance: slow synth masses, vocal apparitions, soft percussive grammar, low harmonic pressure, field material absorbed into the body of the music. A personal idea of music as spiritual perception Olùsìn [Worshippers] by Ibukun sunday   Lagos born, North London based violist, sound artist and electronic composer Ibukun Sunday has slowly shaped one of the most singular languages in contemporary Afro ambient music. His path begins in classical discipline, with viola study from childhood and ensemble experience across chamber and orchestral settings, then opens into field recording, live electronics, noise texture, synthesizer sound and a personal idea of music as spiritual perception. Earlier releases for Phantom Limb’s Spirituals imprint, including The Last Wave and Mantra, placed him in dialogue with philosophy, apocalypse, Vedic thought and Nigerian memory; Harmony / Balance, issued in 2024, carried that research into a wider frame, where drone, melody and existential inquiry moved as a single organism. Olùsìn [Worshippers] now gives this practice its most concentrated form. The album is presented as a devotional ambient work rooted in West African rhythmic tradition, and the definition is useful only as an entrance. Sunday is dealing with faith as vibration, with praise as a form of breath made audible. The record moves with the gravity of a procession seen from a great distance: slow synth masses, vocal apparitions, soft percussive grammar, low harmonic pressure, field material absorbed into the body of the music. Everything advances through recurrence. Motifs return as if memory had learned to sing in circles. Rhythm rarely asks for attention directly; it glows under the surface, ticks inside consonants, gathers in small pulses, then expands into a shared heartbeat. “Rhythm rarely asks for attention directly; it glows under the surface, ticks inside consonants, gathers in small pulses, then expands into a shared heartbeat.” ~Mirco Salvadori What makes Olùsìn [Worshippers] so persuasive is the way Sunday refuses decorative spirituality. The music carries devotion through craft. The choral tones are gauzy and spectral, yet their placement feels almost architectural. The bass frequencies hold a stern calm, the upper harmonics shimmer with a pale organ light, and the voices seem less like singers than traces of people gathered in the same act of listening. At moments the album approaches the suspended radiance of church music, at others it returns to earth through grain, breath, thud and sampled speech. The sacred quality comes through pressure and patience, through the decision to let each sound reveal its weight. A record of rare poise: luminous, grounded, inwardly ecstatic :: Across the eight pieces, Sunday treats the studio as a vessel for collective energy. The titles suggest elemental conditions: whisper, echo, amen, breeze, ages, devotion, hill, edge. They function as points in a wider rite of perception, each one carrying a small emotional temperature. The opening half favors deep resonance and vocal haze, with melodies rising like thin beams through the darkened density of the drones. The central section grows warmer, richer, almost tactile, allowing the listener to sense the body behind the electronics. Toward the final stretch, plucked synthetic figures and trembling harmonic patterns introduce a sharper contour, as if prayer had become a lattice of light. “Amen,” already chosen as the first public signal from the record, offers the clearest key to Sunday’s method. A vocal fragment, full of sibilant motion and West African cadence, becomes rhythm before it becomes meaning. Around it, the synths swell with organ like solemnity, and the piece turns into a compact ceremony of ascent. Edge, near the end, works through Karplus Strong pizzicato logic, its plucked particles layering into a bright, nervous mesh. These moments reveal how Sunday thinks: he begins from pulse, timbre, oral memory and instrumental knowledge, then lets technology behave like a devotional instrument. The machine serves breath, fingers, choir, dust, air. “For an American listener trained by the genealogies of minimalism, gospel resonance, fourth world drift, post Eno ambient and contemporary sound art, Sunday’s record opens a different line of descent.” ~Mirco Salvadori There is also a quiet severity in this album. Its beauty arrives through restraint. Sunday’s classical background is audible in his sense of proportion, in the way he allows harmonic fields to bloom, fade, gather again, and in the discipline with which he keeps the palette reduced. Many ambient records seek immersion through endless expansion; Olùsìn [Worshippers] achieves depth through measure. It feels carved from a few essential elements, each one placed where silence can give it force. The percussion is subtle, the voices are veiled, the field recordings are folded into the fabric, and the melodic cells move with the humility of repeated prayer. For an American listener trained by the genealogies of minimalism, gospel resonance, fourth world drift, post Eno ambient and contemporary sound art, Sunday’s record opens a different line of descent. Its center is West African, diasporic, devotional, intimate, communal. It carries the discipline of the violist, the patience of the field recordist, the concentration of the producer and the listening ethics of an artist who has spoken of sound as a soul language. Olùsìn [Worshippers] asks for attention as participation. It turns worship into acoustic matter, praise into frequency, solitude into chorus. In doing so, Ibukun Sunday has made a record of rare poise: luminous, grounded, inwardly ecstatic, and quietly radical in its faith that sound can still carry human presence beyond explanation. items.body: Empire of Sand provides impeccably built darkened droning soundscapes with an emotional and nihilistic apex. The whole sonic architecture is centered on assaultive, multi-layered harsh electric guitar patterns; micro-noisy, grainy ambient electronics; and a grandiose, spellbinding dystopian cinematic component. Dedicated to the defense of extreme music Ksenza Records is an undisputed key indie label dedicated to the defense of extreme music, from merciless (post-)metal subgenres to deep ambient music, electro-cinematic spells, and abstract noise. I’m familiar with part of their catalogue, including releases by Nytt Land, who have also published major works on Cold Spring (U.K.), as well as Sutekh Hexen and Thisquietarmy. This collaborative effort is the result of a groundbreaking artistic meeting between Nimh (the project of pioneering Italian post-industrial and ethno-ritual drone musician Giuseppe Verticchio) and Sleepwalker (the project of the mastering engineer behind Ksenza). Empire of Sand provides impeccably built darkened droning soundscapes with an emotional and nihilistic apex. The whole sonic architecture is centered on assaultive, multi-layered harsh electric guitar patterns; micro-noisy, grainy ambient electronics; and a grandiose, spellbinding dystopian cinematic component. The brooding and elegantly evocative moving pieces lead the listener into a dense metaphysical post-human world surrounded by decaying fortresses, aural figures from the past, forlorn mythological creatures, ghoulish presences, and tearful angels. Some moments of lightness and serenity occasionally emerge from the desolate, isolationist sensorial bath, as in the elegiac gothadelic anthem “Empire of Sand” and the ascending “The Endless Journey.” The perfect bleak soundtrack for an immersion into ominous sci-fi novels depicting subterranean, cold, anguished, demonic, fearful, and paroxysmal worlds at the border between real and imaginary time, notably found in the classic books of M. P. Shiel, C. Ashton Smith, N. Henneberg, and R. W. Chambers. An awe-inspiring album that is a highly recommended addition for those who enjoy mystical and dark musical odysseys where organic ambient meets drone metal and entrancing noise. Fans of Monocube, Shrine, Nadja, Locrian, Khanate, and similar artists won’t be disappointed. Empire of Sand is available on Ksenza. items.body: In 2024, Elaha Soroor and members of Kefaya performed at a celebration of Hazara culture in Vienna, where posters advertising the event were torn from walls across the city, in what read as an attempt to silence it. The Hazara are a mostly Shia minority who have endured more than a century of persecution in Afghanistan, much of the community scattered into exile, which is why celebrating that culture abroad can still draw hostility. “A Bright Gaze – Negahe Roshan” came out of what followed: the solidarity and unexpected friendships that gathered around the musicians. It is the one bright stretch on Our Freedoms Must Be Won – Azadi Kho Bigri, an album otherwise built on exile and displacement, out this July on the band’s own label, Radio International. The track is built on a 7/8 Afghan folk rhythm, then set inside a synth-rock frame. The guitar carries folk and blues inflections over a warm bank of analogue synthesiser, while synth lines answer Soroor’s voice in call-and-response. The band put the arrangement together through improvisation, which gives it a quick, unforced momentum. Soroor grew up between Iran and Afghanistan and rose to national attention as a finalist on the television contest Afghan Star, the first female Hazara singer to perform on Afghan television. After she used her platform to condemn the stoning law, death threats forced her out of the country, and she rebuilt her music in London. Kefaya, the London trio of guitarist Giuliano Modarelli, keys player Al MacSween and drummer Joost Hendrickx, take their name from the Arabic word for enough, a cry that ran through the Arab Spring. Modarelli and MacSween started the group in 2012 and built their 2016 debut, Radio International, from sessions tracked across India, Palestine, Italy and Spain, wiring folk traditions to electronics and threading political voices through the mix. They first worked with Soroor on 2019’s Songs of Our Mothers, reworking Afghan women’s songs into something harder and more electronic. Stream “A Bright Gaze” HERE, and get a copy of Our Freedoms Must Be Won on vinyl and digital through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Kefaya & Elaha Soroor – A Bright Gaze appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 4.5 starsIf you have your musical head permanently screwed on back-to-front, with a head spun full of fantastical musical aberrations, then this is a band for you. This is not for the faint of heart, but those of us with a disposition for all things out there. There is much rewarding music bound up in this avant-garde album, well worth checking out.�I believe that this is the band/artist's 21st album. There are many influences, with everything from the earlier days of prog rock right up to some almost metal like lines of guitar work, but only in small doses. Athak is yet another virtually unknown band, that is turning out some really high-quality music, that is going by unnoticed, by pretty much everybody.This is probably some of the easier to listen to Zeuhl music than many groups within the genre are offering. With a fair amount of oriental folk music, some quite western modern classical piano, operatic vocals and an overall heavy sound that never really feels metallic. It is one to stick the headphones on for and zone out with all the creativity on offer for the full one hour, twelve minutes.Well, recommended to all who like music to sound spontaneous as well as thought out all at the same time.

items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — And The Light is shining in the darkness, and the darkness did not overtake it.SLUG COMPARISON"Slug Comparison is the solo project of Canadian artist Doug Harrison, primarily known as the vocalist for progressive rock/metal band, Fen."- from the artist's bio.Credits:Doug Harrison: vocals, guitar, bass, programmingRandall Stoll: drumsAll songs written and produced by Doug Harrison.And may I say, here are some impressions of this impeccable EP: Somber. Thoughtful. Melancholy. Dark, with faint traces of light. Moody. Rich with meaning and texture and depth. Music and lyrics germane, inextricable, worth pondering. Not a note or chord or lyric or vocal line misplaced or overplayed or unnecessary. Evocative."Cold In Cold Out""Cold in cold out/ that's how it goes/ in with a cry/ and out with a moan"?This EP has six tracks playing for a total time of twenty-six minutes, forty-two seconds.Yet in the best possible way, it seems much longer, and much shorter than that."Much longer", because there is so much packed into each song, so much emotion, so much to ponder, so much complexity even while on the surface seeming so simple, so much heart and soul and mind and body."Much shorter", because when the listener gets into the flow, discovers the moods and rhythms and sensibilities of each song- it seems over almost before it began.Consider the title itself, "Cold In Cold Out". Frankly, I don't get the sense that Doug Harrison commits to paper, then to tape, then on to the next iterations of music, anything that is extraneous or throw-away or superfluous.What- You Thought I Would Explain it All?All right- since you're paying me good money to write this review (well, then again, maybe not)- I think this EP is a meditation on death, heartache, birth, betrayal?and some faint signs of hope, wrapped within beguiling, sonorous, melodic music, and helmed by the wistful, powerful, emotive, tender voice of Harrison telling his truths.For me, birth and death can be cold things- the baby abruptly expelled into the buzzing, blooming world from her nourishing, safe womb. And, the brave soul who feels the breath of the reaper coming ever closer, who finds the tongue of the hollow seeking to suck the life force from the increasingly vulnerable husk.Look again and think about the album art pictured above: the enormous full moon, the umbilical cord/root system trailing toward the fallen traveler, the spectral hills, the blooming night flowers and ferns, the clouds with silver linings.And the opening track, "Tongue of the Hollow"- who is singing to us of dying (and being evocative, how is it that this instantly makes me recall my mother's dying- her reaching for things only she could see in the air, her slowly wasting away yet her life-breaths which she did not wish to relinquish)? Why is it that I recalled my sister and I needing to make decisions about mother's few remaining things, even before she died- and feeling like some kind of heartless parasite removing them one by one?Who is "the stranger above whose footsteps creak in beautiful time"?And all of it set in this solemn, somber tune, austere classical guitar, simple but powerful drumming, building, growing?"oh when the melody pours its wine/ out of the body, out of the mind", and the stranger stepping once more "to beautiful song"."To Whom Would You Answer"My point is, when I raise the question of "the voice" within the lyrics, about who is saying these things, to whom, and in what context, I'm saying that these, in concert with the way the song is constructed, create a tiny "universe" that requires thought, attention, and care- all of which I find refreshing and challenging!I "hear" Doug Harrison's music as an intensely absorbing example of these qualities. Musically, in "To Whom Would You Answer", we hear the hushed, restrained voice issuing languid menace to the unidentified recipient, who is being threatened with humiliation and perhaps liquidation. The wah-guitar tones suggest the ambiguity of the piece. The gritty bass and pulsing drums in verse two highlight how Harrison uses tonal shift in subtle or obvious ways to drive the music and the message. The octave vocals later also create menace and melancholy- Harrison clearly thinks through every aspect and every line- and I wonder, as an old musician, how crazy he drives himself trying to get things "right".And to whom WILL you answer, especially if these self-same accusers paradoxically lionize you? Hang your face on the wall?"Back to the World"A few noteworthy things about this track- it starts with a much lighter touch, and the listener is nearly relieved that the ominous and dark tones of the album might be mitigated with some light and hope. We hear a lighter guitar line, clean chords, melodic voice, clear guitar lead.HOWEVER (listen up to the lyrics, dang it) the protagonist seems to be encountering a past love and finding a mix of gladness at seeing her again, and shame for earlier not being there for her: "good seeing you out again/ on a day I thought was ruined", and then, "I never did one drop for you/ just outta my hands ignored you" and, "you fought black wind on a ledge/ I dropped my eyes/ and hung my head".And this exquisite line, "you've come back to the world/ when I'm all but missing from my life?and I'm dressed like some [%*!#] I don't like".Similarly in "Burden of Life", we hear the hushed voice, the picked clean guitar, the fuller band sound enters with drum and bass, becoming elegiac as the clean guitar lead sings- all of which concerns what sounds like a person on his/her deathbed aware of being unaware, bearing the burden of life and wishing to drop it.One of those passages made me think of my dad on his deathbed- after years of polio and later post-polio which eventually rendered him nearly immobile, and the devastating lyrics, "you knew an end was coming to the/ steady roll of your stride/ through golden beams falling from/ the sky/ you trampled down the doubt/ anyone could see in you the hope to/ lose that trouble close behind".My father did limp- gracefully- through golden beams falling from the sky, and was ready, oh, so ready to release the burden of life, the trouble close behind.Title TrackSo, I feel like posting ALL the lyrics on this track, they're that revealing, and tough, and tender, explanatory, and difficult.Which is one reason "Cold In Cold Out" is my favorite song of this outstanding EP- that plus the way it begins with a gentle classical guitar backing Harrison's most vulnerable vocals? then it grows, and grows, and builds.Let these lyrics suffice: "The path is a tangle of flowers and thorns/ of those who would bleed you/ and those who seem warm/ together you roam/ (CHORUS 1) and follow the light/ over the ground/ you ferry your bones/ all secretly asking/ when can we put the load down?"It struck me that the gorgeous full moon pictured is yet a reflection of the light of the sizzling sun, the life-giving sun. The journey is not without light; still, it is a journey with one final destination.The heart-wrenching chorus has three iterations, each more intense, building into almost unbearable loveliness and tragedy, in which Mr. Harrison shows his incredible vocal range, and we hear some cool bass guitar work after chorus two.We also get some gutsy power chords as an exquisite counterpoint to the gentle classical guitar.When can we put this load down? Cold in cold out.No HealerTime heals all wounds? Not this wound, no. Although I don't think of this EP as a single-concept album, it certainly has congruent threads, and as the final track, this one leaves a rather dark energy trailing.Although at first we hear, "no healer will come but the passage of time", later the narrator changes it to this: "no healer will come through the passage of time." On this track there are suggestions of dissonance in the swirling electric guitar passages, and the trippy lead guitar lines can seem almost dizzying.I've noticed in Doug Harrison's music a deep tie with the natural world, suggesting that all are tied into one long cord of life and death, living and dying. On "No Healer", we get the suggestion that the dying traveler becomes food and fuel for other species- and in this way, perhaps, life goes on.The light is shining, and the darkness does not comprehend it.In ConclusionIn short order, Doug Harrison via his side project, SLUG COMPARISON, returns with this stellar EP, set to release 09/10/2026- because of its lyrical depth and musical ingenuity, I consider this an excellent addition to any progressive rock collection.

Alberto Rigoni (Jeff Scott Soto, Jordan Rudess, Marco Minnemann, Gavin Harrison), Michael Manring (Spastic Ink, Alex Skolnik/Skol Patrol, Attention Deficit, Steve Morse, Alex De Grassi, Will Ackerman and others) and Stuart (Stu) Hamm (Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, Frank Gambale) are the bassists an
items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicked 4, but really a bit better at 4.25.Let's call this one, back to "Bass-ics" as this album features three of the world's top bassists in a collaboration called "Dystopia". Alberto Rigoni (Jeff Scott Soto, Jordan Rudess, Marco Minnemann, Gavin Harrison), Michael Manring (Spastic Ink, Alex Skolnik/Skol Patrol, Attention Deficit, Steve Morse, Alex De Grassi, Will Ackerman and others) and Stuart (Stu) Hamm (Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, Frank Gambale) are the bassists and they are augmented by drummers Tim "Herb" Alexander (Primus) and David Menoudakis (Motion Device). Rigoni is the album's producer.The album comes courtesy of the all-around awesome guy Nick Katona (the man has style!) and his label Melodic Revolution Records (MMR). It was released on February 27, 2026. I look forward to reviewing more music released by this label. As always, this is a cold listen, I receive no additional compensation, and I call it like I hear it. The only frame of reference I have going into this is "Fish Out of Water" by the late, great Chris Squire, but this album is a fully instrumental affair, so it should be interesting. Without further ado, let's get down deep into it.Track 1 - Genesis (4:26)A moderately slow chordal pattern starts off the track, and a cool drum groove comes in with a polyrhythmic pattern. At around 1 minute in, they lock into a groove. They are using some effects that make some of the bass notes sound almost brass-like; very cool. The drums play some amazing fills. The groove changes at around 3:25. I don't know which bassist is playing what, but there was a cool lead break near the ending. Great tune!Track 2 - The Algorithm (3:16)This begins with droning sounds, onto which a fretless bass plays an opening tune. So far there are no drums on this and it is very atmospheric. I wonder if one or more of them is using a synth pickup module to create some of these sounds. Nice soundscape track.Track 3 - Entropia (3:55)This one has a jazzy groove to it, with shifting meters. It's very proggy! Lots of great rhythms here. There is a melodic hook. Cool bass and drum synchronicity at around 3:20 on a morse code rhythm. I like it!Track 4 - Limbo (3:59)This fades in with some foreboding sounds. No drums on this one. There is a sense of motion, however, caused by the rhythms. One of the basses takes on a piano-like tone. There are some unique effects in the later part of the track. Pretty interesting.Track 5 - Solar (3:27)I like the descending, chord-melody thing that they start with here. The drums are back in a big way here. I like the changing melodies and grooves throughout this track. These guys are definitely among the best in the world and are showing it on this track. Great drum solo after 3 minutes. One of my favorites from the album, I'd say!Track 6 - Ethereal Horizon (2:34)Bass harmonics are featured as this one begins. The synth-like tones are back; maybe a whammy pedal? They are certainly re-defining what the bass can do here. Track 7 - Dystopia (8:46)The final/title track is the longest, so let's call it a closing epic. A rhythm pattern with drums is established quickly. At around 1:30 one of the guys takes on a lead guitar type tone, which is later harmonized with another player; they use a distortion effect. Following that, there is a really cool canon-like section with the three playing overlapping tunes. Great drum grooves on this as well. They really take us through several grooves and moods. I love the groove that kicks in at around the 5-minute mark. I like the slow harmonies as they approach the 7-minute mark; gradually all 3 of them take part in the chords, and there are overdubs as well as it keeps building. It is a rich, brassy tone they are creating. The bass can create many timbres and they show it here. The only thing missing for me is a final punctuation for the ending, as it just kind of stopped. Otherwise, this is clearly the flag-ship track of the album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is a fairly short album at around 31 minutes, perhaps we should call it an EP. Regardless, this is an entertaining way to spend half an hour and see what three master-bassists (sorry, I'll go sit in the corner now?) can do. It was an interesting experiment and yielded some cool results. I have no Idea whether they are planning to follow-up with more releases, but it's worth checking out. I'll give this a respectable 4.25 out of 5, or 85%. Thanks again to Nick Katona and MRR for providing me with this music for review. I expect there be more in the not-too-distant future.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Locande delle fate is a band which I had not heard of until an acquaintance of mine recommended themto me after chatting about prog and jazz for a while, evidently as I do, I postponed listening toany of their records until I finished some pending ones, now I have listened to this record, "HomoHomini Lupus" twice, and I'm eager to say the many things I think about this particular record,which, are not very positive if I'm to be very honest.I'd like to address that, I do not speak Italian, and while Spanish and Italian do share a ton ofgrammar, words and common origin from latin, I did not fully understand the lyrics because of thislanguage barrier, judging by the overview I did indeed understand, this is a concept album, which isapparent and obvious mainly by the track titles, despite this, I will not analyze the lyrical aspectof the record any further since I'm not in a position to do so.This record is quite different from your average RPI record in the sense that, it's notgrandiloquent, baroque, theatrical and Mediterranean sounding, I'd like to say that something thatmakes a record great is sticking to it's cultural roots and sound while innovating and expandingit's foundations...Homo Homini Lupus DOES NOT do that, it splits from the Italian roots that madeRPI great in the first place, and tries to mimic Anglo-Saxon rock and pop. The quality of thecompositions is very poor, the tracks are mostly bland and dull, nothing really fits completely, itsits in an uncanny valley : trying to mimic someone else while trying to pretend you have notabandoned your identity. The instruments are simple, just hour typical line up of some keys,guitars, bass guitars and drums, sometimes less is more, but this is not the case, they feeldisconnected both musically and emotionally...almost as a watered down Alan Parsons project, which Iwill asume was a big inspiration for Locanda delle fate's creative process.Despite the musicians and singer being very talented, they still feel plain, they sound as if theywere not motivated, the singer's high pitched vocals are also unbearable most of the time, they trybeing dramatic..maybe they tried TOO hard, and too much of anything is never any good.The production is also dull, not balanced, poorly equalized, inconsistent between tracks (whichworsens the fact that all songs, are almost the same in composition, and this productioninconsistency does not help at all), and the guitar tones are simply just too exaggerated.For the quality this record has, it could have been 10 or 15 minutes shorter and no one wouldcomplain really, it's a record that disappoints, specially since it is part of one of the best progsub genres...really, I wouldn't listen to it again, and I urge you that, if you want to listen toany other record by Locanda delle fate, follow the advice of other reviewers and avoid this record,go straight into their debut album.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Echoes And Signals: a blend of techno-prog-math and experimental post-new-wave?or at least, that's how I like to describe them."Simulacra" begins with a brooding atmosphere?wailing guitars and a melancholic sound blending post-rock, math-rock, and crossover styles with a touch of Wilson-esque psychedelia. It's a musical treat to whet the appetite. "Temporal Waves" shifts into dark electro, a monolithic cinematic soundscape weaving through danceable electronics to create a contemplative mood. The guitar solo echoes Porcupine Tree, with notes bursting forth alongside a great riff and an expansive shredding section reminiscent of Randy McStine, all leading into an outro driven by an immersive looper effect. "Cloud Gallery" deepens the atmospheric, spacey sound; the vocals?reminiscent of Radiohead or Eno?float over a backdrop of reverberating synths. A bewitching, groovy guitar dialogue takes hold, leading to an explosive finale driven by a heavy riff and solemn, almost liturgical vocals."Evermore" features acoustic guitar and atmospheric spoken-word vocals, with radiant keyboards; there's a hint of Barclay James Harvest in the mellow, sentimental vibe, while the western-style tones lend a space-psych lament quality. "Singularity" is built on a moody electronic foundation, with accessible synths complementing the soft, melodic guitar. A gradual build-up launches a smooth, captivating crescendo, with Fedor's vocals vibrating with a nonchalant, reverent intensity. At the halfway mark, the musical momentum shifts?a "Berlin School" atmosphere triggers an energetic detour, featuring a long, driving passage where Leo's presence is frantically felt. It concludes with a robotic, vocoded finale set against chilling synths reminiscent of Tangerine Dream?truly surprising.Echoes And Signals represents a philosophical-musical translation?a concept of opposites for an album that exists in the space between, capturing fragments of a shifting reality. A sound that leans towards dark wave, electro, and cinematic post-rock?echoes and signals indeed!

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — With Phil Miller, Pip Pyle, Amanda Parsons, Jimmy Hastings, and the very architect of the Canterbury scene, Dave Stewart, all members of Hatfield and the North, National Health was formed, joined by bassist Neil Murray, who came from Colosseum II and would also work with Bill Bruford during the rehearsals for Feels Good to Me.Right from the start with "Tenemos Roads," there is a distinct energy, stemming from a rhythm section (drums and bass) that leans toward aggressive jazz-rock fusi�n, to which Jimmy Hastings' bass clarinet adds a supernatural, postmodern air, further enhanced by Dave Stewart's keyboards. The jazz-rock turns psychedelic while incorporating a funky groove that keeps things fresh; then Amanda Parsons enters, singing atonally, sounding forever ethereal, like the soundtrack to a gateway into another dimension. Her style differs from how Annette Peacock might sound with Bill Bruford's band, yet she also possesses a quality reminiscent of Sally Oldfield.The music supports her, and subsequently, she supports the music, through both the up-tempo passages and the moments where the action pauses and both the guitar and her voice explore high registers. The composition elevates the piece beyond any single genre. That sense of confusi�n, and the intent of social critique during a turbulent era, also translates into the music and forms an integral part of it.Frank Zappa's One Size Fits All is another essential reference, as are all the bands Stewart was involved with, from Arzachel and Egg, with their classical influences, to the power of Khan alongside Steve Hillage. "Brujo" reveals another facet of the band, featuring Amanda Parsons channeling Annie Haslam; the action is driven simultaneously by her vocals, bass, and keyboards, before shifting into jazz-style improvisation. This album is packed with music, and it shows, as fleeting piano passages give way to keyboards played at breakneck speed that never cease to offer up new melodies, delivering the best of a live concert experience within a studio setting.One could say that the jazz-rock style of "Borogoves" is certainly obscure and intricate, perhaps akin to Brand X, yet Dave Stewart plays the clavinet there, bringing back a funky feel, while Phil Miller's distorted guitar seems to weave through the spaces left open for it. However, its follow-up, "Borogoves, Part One", moves away from those cited references; once again, it is the composition itself that lends the piece its distinctive character and individuality. There is a martial, existentialist quality to the music, heightened, of course, by Amanda Parsons' vocals.Following an initial cacophony of keyboards, "Elephants" serves as a showcase for Phil Miller, before Dave Stewart alternates with his own prowess on acoustic and electric piano, joined by Nick Levitt's synthesizers, delivering fusion riffs that would not only set a precedent but define an era. Jazz-rock had never come so close to being orchestral and symphonic, at least not within the sonic framework established by National Health on their debut, which was rooted in the Canterbury compositional style.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many versions of Soft Machine, but only one Allan Holdsworth. There is the Soft Machine of Kevin Ayers, the one with Robert Wyatt, the era featuring Mike Ratledge and Elton Dean, and the later period with Karl Jenkins. Yet Holdsworth brought his signature sound to groups like Tony Williams' Lifetime and Nucleus, as well as later projects such as U.K. and Bill Bruford's solo band. Which brings us to Bundles, where he would also share the bill with bassist Roy Babbington, with whom he had worked on the 1972 Nucleus album Belladonna.While the style of fusion they were developing was already becoming increasingly electrified, Holdsworth's arrival brought powerful riffs that, combined with Mike Ratledge's synthesizers and organ, shaped the main suite, "Hazard Profile." The guitar scales are underpinned by Roy Babbington's tireless bass and Rhodes piano notes that drift like butterflies against the sky of 1975; the truly transcendent moment is the ensuing sequence, aided by the organ, which turns Holdsworth's notes like the pages of a book, gathering layer upon layer of information. One page features virtuosic guitar work that invites us to follow along; another presents piano and acoustic guitar in the suite's second part, capturing the poetic spirit of the era; the fourth section is more intense, almost reminiscent of Cream, save for the syncopated drum rhythm driving the tempo, setting the stage to accelerate into the fifth and final movement, where Karl Jenkins enters on the saxophone.After "Gone Sailing", a track with echoes of Ralph Towner, "Bundles" resumes the initial quest; the guitar navigates curves and corners, venturing into every nook and cranny with clockwork precisi�n, where the drum cymbals act as alarms and the bass serves as the second hand, tirelessly marking the relentless passage of time. The momentum never falters, not even for Holdsworth as "Land of the Bag Snake" begins, since the tracks are seamlessly linked, much like the flowers and privet hedge on the album cover, forming a unified whole where butterflies take flight; "The Man Who Waved at Trains" then continues the journey, albeit at a slower, steady, jazz-infused pace.Karl Jenkins and his oboe provided the missing touch, casting a spell over that timeless afternoon, an afternoon of backyards, plants, and sunshine. Much like on the debut album, the tracks unfold like pages turned by the wind, one after another; amidst this rhythm, Peff enters with keyboards and saxophone, conjuring a dreamlike, otherworldly atmosphere. Where did the violence go? Where did this calm, reminiscent of an endless siesta, come from? It returns through those same instruments, though momentarily clouded by the all-consuming, eternal keyboard. Mike Ratledge and Karl Jenkins vie for the spotlight in the finale, a tour de force where neither truly wins, for the real victor is Soft Machine. "The Floating World" serves as a sort of electronic elegy, a chance to catch one's breath after a relentless journey, an experience that was far from wasted, however, for it undoubtedly leaves the spirit feeling truly fulfilled.

items.body: For Swedish post-punk and goth rock stalwarts Then Comes Silence, songwriting works best when it carries a little danger in its coat pocket, along with a nightclub flyer, a bent cigarette, and perhaps the phone number of somebody your mother warned you about. On Judgement Day, the Stockholm trio take that instinct and feed it through a bright synth opening that sounds almost indecently cheerful before the floor gives way beneath it. The melody initially suggests a lost continental dance hit, polished enough to wander into an airport lounge without being questioned. Then Alex Svenson’s voice enters, carrying the moral weight of a man reading names from a very unpleasant guest list, while Jonas Fransson’s drums and Hugo Zombie’s guitar tighten the track into a stern, muscular march. Clan of Xymox, Killing Joke, and The Chameleons provide useful reference points, though Then Comes Silence retain their own heavy-footed grandeur, where every bass note seems dressed for a funeral, and every hook reads like a majestic elegy for the human race. “This song is about failure, bad decisions and poor behaviour – those who will be the first in line on doomsday,” the band explains. The humor—or perhaps the confession—resides in the arrangement. By featuring an almost alien electronic motif at the outset, the trio playfully embeds their own musical misbehavior, all while enjoying the process. Then Comes Silence greet the end with a crooked smile, loosening goth’s funeral tie and sparing Judgement Day the pallbearer solemnity so often mistaken for depth. Director Damon Zurawski of Future Legends Films places the band among dancers drawn from the gothic scene, creating a performance video that feels communal without sanding down the song’s severity. Svenson commands the center with bass in hand, Fransson drives from behind the kit, and Zombie cuts through the room with economical force. The dancers supply movement, personality, and proof that black clothing contains more shades than most paint stores. Watch the video for Judgement Day below: Judgement Day introduces Requiem Ballroom, due out on November 20th on Metropolis Records. The album follows 2024’s Trickery, a record Classic Rock described as “the post-punk influence of Bauhaus or Joy Division offset by an ’80s windblown, cinematic sense of drama presented with silky production and confidence.” Vive Le Rock concurred, remarking on its “huge, spectral sound that cascades the post-punk genres seamlessly whilst delivering a unique and compelling sound that is as captivatingly gripping as it is intense.” After years of stages shared with Fields of the Nephilim, Clan of Xymox, Chameleons, and A Place to Bury Strangers, Then Comes Silence sound firmly in possession of their machinery. Judgement Day turns failure into propulsion, poor behavior into choreography, and doomsday into a club night worth attending before the lights come up and the bill inevitably comes due at dawn. Then Comes Silence are on tour in mainland Europe in August and September, including an appearance at the M’era Luna Festival in Hildesheim, Germany on 9th August. items.body: I’m taking a ride with my best friend’s girlfriend, and she used to be mine. Love crime. Detroit duo Credit Card make music for the hour when the club floor has acquired the adhesive properties of flypaper, the strobe has erased everyone’s face, and somebody in a leather jacket is conducting a one-sided argument with a subwoofer. Their new single, Love Crime, finds Shaun Hunter handling vocals, synth, and noise while Max Dameron supplies programming, synth, and guitar. Together, they turn romantic misconduct into a hard, queasy sprint through downtown. Love Crime is the second single from Credit Card’s forthcoming debut album, Devil’s Night / Dead Internet, due August 14, 2026. The title suggests either a municipal emergency or the browser history of a recently divorced nightclub promoter, which is more or less the territory the duo occupies. Their synth punk is aggressive, distorted, and built for physical response, though the song’s real pressure comes from the dawning suspicion that desire has selected the worst available route and locked the doors, and nobody involved appears eager to slow down. The sludginess of their sound brings to mind Nine Inch Nails as well as the Soft Moon – it is hypnotic in is raw power. The setup is luridly simple. A man takes a nighttime drive with his best friend’s girlfriend, who also happens to be his former lover. Betrayal, jealousy, and old possession rights crowd into the back seat, where nobody has remembered to fasten a seat belt. The ride carries the thrill of stolen intimacy, yet every beat pushes the characters closer to the embarrassing conclusion that wanting someone can be less a grand passion than a very efficient method of ruining several friendships at once. Hunter delivers the vocal with a cold, accusatory focus, sounding equally implicated and appalled. Dameron’s programming presses forward in blunt mechanical surges, while the synths bend around the rhythm with sinister, sinuous purpose. Guitar and noise roughen the edges without smothering the hook. The result feels immediate and dangerous, like overhearing a confession through the bathroom wall and realizing the names are familiar. On Love Crime, Credit Card makes bad judgment sound fast, stylish, and briefly irresistible. The song understands that romance often provides its own getaway vehicle, though it remains notably unreliable when the police lights appear in the mirror. Listen to Love Crime below and order the single here. Devil’s Night / Dead Internet by CREDIT CARDCredit Card has been building considerable attention in Detroit through shows governed by strobe lights, mosh pits, leather jackets, and beats capable of troubling nearby foundations. Their first seven-inch single, “(CC)” (a Germs reference) sold out at its release show, leaving the group with the enviable problem of having insufficient merchandise and an increasingly attentive audience. Credit Card is readying their debut “mixtape” for a Summer 2026 release, and local crowds in Detroit already sound eager to be flattened by it. Follow Credit Card: Instagram Bandcamp The post “Let’s Go for a Ride” — Detroit Industrial-Punk Duo Credit Card Shares New Single “Love Crime” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Los Angeles electro-pop duo Tart Vandelay releases its debut album, “Odyssey”, independently on August 7, 2026, on all streaming platforms. The record, made by musical couple Kate Halligan and Marty LoFaso, brings together eleven tracks written and developed over nearly ten years. Halligan stated: “This album is almost like a child to us. It grew up alongside us. Each song captures a different phase of our lives, our relationship, and our evolution as artists and as people. It’s about sharing our art and spreading good vibes to our audience.” LoFaso stated: “Odyssey is proof that it’s worth patiently pursuing a dream. We’re incredibly happy to finally present this first chapter of our story.” ‘Spin,’ ‘Bells’ and ‘Starlight’ lead into ‘Odyssey’ Tart Vandelay built up to “Odyssey” with a run of singles, each presenting a different side of the duo’s sound. “Spin” and “Bells” arrived first, followed by “Starlight,” the final single before the album and, according to the band, the song that ended up setting the creative direction for the whole record. “Starlight” combines synthesizers and pop melodies in an arrangement that balances retro-leaning tones with contemporary production. Across “Odyssey,” the duo mixes synth-pop, electronic indie and contemporary disco into a single identity. “Bells,” the most recent single before “Odyssey,” is available to stream below. About Tart Vandelay Tart Vandelay formed in 2014 when Kate Halligan and Marty LoFaso began writing songs together while studying in Boston; the pair transferred to Berklee College of Music, where Halligan studied songwriting and LoFaso studied music business. The duo later moved to Halligan and LoFaso’s home region in the Northeast before relocating to Phoenix, Arizona, and eventually to Los Angeles, California, where they are now based. Along the way they released the EP “Janus” (2019) and singles including “Luv Who U R” (2021), “DJ Play My Song” (2021), “R U Mine?” (2022) and “I’m Dreaming” (2024), building an independent career around a sound that mixes synth-pop, electronic indie and contemporary disco. In 2026, the singles “Spin” and “Bells” led into “Starlight,” the final single ahead of “Odyssey,” the duo’s debut studio album, released independently on August 7, 2026.

items.body: La Division Technique, the French electronics project of Philippe Saintlos, releases “L’inversion des pôles” with Pascal Comelade as a limited, numbered 7″ vinyl edition of 200 copies through Ubahn. The record is out now. L’inversion des pôles by La Division Technique avec Pascal Comelade La Division Technique and Comelade press two tracks to a numbered 7 inch “L’inversion des pôles” holds two tracks, “Anaphores” on the A side and “Syncopes” on the B side, both composed by Comelade and Saintlos. Comelade plays grand piano, vertical piano, Farfisa organ, an Emenee plastic guitar and a Roland RD 300 SX keyboard, with “Syncopes” adding an EMS-AKS synthesizer and a Koma Elektronik FT201. Saintlos contributes a Korg MS10, an Arturia MiniBrute, a Nord Lead X2, a Yamaha RX11 drum machine, an ARP Odyssey and a Poly D clone Minimoog. The two recorded the pair of tracks with Raph Dumas between November 2024 and April 2026; Dumas also mastered the release, and Saintlos produced it and designed the sleeve. Each of the 200 copies is individually numbered. About La Division Technique La Division Technique is an electronics project from France, founded and directed by Philippe Saintlos, built around old-school electronics, dark soundscapes, minimal synths and industrial-ambient textures played on analog synthesizers, filters, guitars, voices and spatial sound recordings. A 2017 meeting with the label Rotorelief led to the release of the album “Unexpected Works, Random Systems,” drawn from tape recordings dating to the 1980s. A second album, “Nebula,” followed in 2019 on Rotorelief and Ubahn. The project returned in 2023 with “Traversant les cités liquides,” and issued “Tristes Machines,” its fourth album, on Ubahn in 2025, alongside the 2024 single “A Beginners Guide to Brian Eno…Baby’s On Fire.” Saintlos has also co-founded the labels Ditec, Semantic and Odessa. Pascal Comelade, born in Montpellier in 1955, is a self-taught French Catalan musician who debuted with the electronic-leaning album “Fluences,” influenced by Heldon, before building a body of work centered on toy instruments played through his Bel Canto Orquestra; he has recorded with Robert Wyatt, Faust, Christophe Miossec and P.J. Harvey among others. His work with La Division Technique on “L’inversion des pôles” pairs his toy-instrument and acoustic keyboard playing with Saintlos’s analog synthesizer sound.
